title: Caring for a Cold or Flu at Home
hook: Most colds and flu run their course on their own. Good home care is about comfort and rest — and knowing the handful of red flags that mean it's time to get checked.
key_points: Rest and drink plenty of fluids while your body fights the virus.
Over-the-counter remedies can ease fever, aches, and congestion.
Antibiotics don't work on viruses like colds and flu.
See a doctor for trouble breathing, chest pain, or symptoms that worsen.
content_html: Colds and flu are caused by viruses, and for most healthy adults they clear up on their own within a week or two. Home care can't cure them faster, but it can make you a lot more comfortable while your immune system does the work.
extra_html: The NHS advice for self-care is reassuringly low-tech: rest, stay well hydrated, and use over-the-counter remedies to ease symptoms like fever, body aches, sore throat, and a blocked nose. Crucially, antibiotics target bacteria and do nothing for viral illnesses like the common cold or flu — taking them when they aren't needed only fuels antibiotic resistance. What matters most is recognizing when self-care isn't enough. The NHS flags warning signs such as difficulty breathing, chest pain, symptoms that persist or worsen rather than improving, or being in a higher-risk group. If any of those apply, contact your provider or a health advice line rather than waiting it out.

related.title: Cold, Flu, or COVID?
related.hook: They share a lot of symptoms, but colds, flu, and COVID-19 differ in how fast they hit and how hard — and telling them apart can change what you do next.

related.title: When a Symptom Needs a Doctor
related.hook: Most everyday symptoms pass on their own. The skill worth having is recognizing the red flags that mean don't wait — call for help now.

related.title: Antibiotics: Use Them Right
related.hook: Antibiotics are miracle drugs against bacteria — and useless against viruses like colds and flu. Using them when they won't help fuels a genuinely dangerous problem.

related.title: Using Pain Relievers Safely
related.hook: The pain relievers in your medicine cabinet are safe used right — and surprisingly risky used wrong. Knowing the two main types and their limits is the whole game.

flashcards.prompt: Why won't antibiotics help an ordinary cold or flu?

choices.text: Colds and flu are caused by viruses, which antibiotics don't treat
Antibiotics only work if started within an hour of symptoms
Antibiotics are only for children, not adults

flashcards.explanation_html: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses. Colds and flu are viral, so antibiotics don't help and using them needlessly contributes to resistance.

flashcards.prompt: What are the basics of caring for a cold or flu at home?
flashcards.back_html: Rest and drink plenty of fluids while the virus runs its course, and use over-the-counter remedies for fever, aches, and congestion if needed. Seek care if you have trouble breathing, chest pain, or symptoms that get worse instead of better.
